title: Telling the Whole Story
overview: This is the last unit of the level, and it puts the whole level together. You will tell one long account: the background, what happened, the people in it, and what you made of it. You will put two past actions side by side and say what has only now happened. You will add extra detail between commas, describe a thing with three words, and judge how it went. At the end you gather work from four earlier units into one portfolio, and take the A2 check across the four skills.
learningPath: Meet 24 words for joining an account, the people in it, looking back and judging it.
Read a long personal account, an information page and a real course record card.
Put two past actions side by side with while, was and were.
Say what has only now happened, and what you have done at some point in your life.
Add extra detail about a person between two commas, with whose and whom.
Put three describing words in order, with an -ing or -ed one among them.
Make a comparison stronger with far, much and a lot.
Take the level quiz, do the A2 check in four skills, and build the portfolio.
lectureScript:
Welcome to Unit 20. This is the last unit of the level.
Everything here is for one job: telling the whole story of something that took time.
Not one moment. A whole month, or a whole course, or a whole repair.
You can already tell what happened yesterday. Now you will tell what happened over weeks.
A long account has four parts. Say them with me.
First, the background. What a person needs to know before the story starts.
Second, what happened, in order.
Third, the people in it.
Fourth, what you made of it. Was it worthwhile, or was it disappointing?
Those four parts are the shape of this unit.
Now the first pattern.
Two things went on at the same time. Both take was or were, then a verb with -ing.
While she was driving, I was reading the map.
While I was waiting at the desk, the assistant was looking for my file.
Both halves are long. Neither one stops the other.
You already know one action cutting across another. I was cooking when the power went off.
That one is long and short. This one is long and long. Listen for while.
The second pattern. The present perfect, twice.
One use is what has only now happened. I have just finished the form.
The words are just and recently.
The other use is your whole life up to now. Have you ever done this before? I have never done it.
No date at all. The time is your life.
The third pattern. Extra detail about a person.
My supervisor, whose office is upstairs, signed it on Friday.
Whose means belonging to that person. Whom is used after a small word like with or to.
The client, to whom I sent the card, replied the same day.
When the detail is extra, it sits between two commas. Take it out and the sentence still works.
The fourth pattern. Three describing words in a row.
An impressive old leather chair. A long, tiring, badly planned week.
What you think of it comes first. Then size, then age, then colour, then material.
And one of the three may end in -ing or -ed. Tiring, satisfying, disappointing, finished.
The fifth pattern. Making a comparison stronger.
Better is a comparison. Far better is a stronger one.
It went far better than I expected. It took much longer than the notice said.
Far, much and a lot go in front. They do not go in front of the plain word.
Say much better, not much good.
Now the words. There are twenty-four.
Six join a long account: background, whereas, despite, nevertheless, furthermore, overall.
Whereas puts two different facts side by side. Despite means even though there was a problem.
Six name the people: relative, witness, official, assistant, supervisor, client.
Six look back: experience, achievement, memory, regret, benefit, challenge.
And six judge how it went: successful, effective, worthwhile, disappointing, impressive, satisfying.
One last thing, and it matters.
At the end of this unit there is a check in four skills: listening, reading, speaking and writing.
You will get four results, on four lines. Do not add them together.
One number would hide the skill that needs your time.
Everything in this unit may be invented. A made-up job, a made-up week, a made-up name.
What is being checked is the English, never your life.
Read each part. Say it out loud. Record it. Check it against the key.
Then tell the whole story.

words.meaning: What was happening before, and what a person needs to know first.
words.example: Here is the background: the office moved in March.
practice: Start with the background, then tell what happened.
She gave me the background in two sentences.
Without the background, the story is hard to follow.
The report has a short background at the top.
words.tutor: Tell me a short story with no background at all, and I will ask you the two questions I still need answered.

words.meaning: A word that puts two different facts side by side.
words.example: The first week was quiet, whereas the second was very busy.
practice: I finished early, whereas my colleague stayed until seven.
The old machine was noisy, whereas this one is quiet.
Whereas the morning class was full, the evening one was empty.
He wanted to wait, whereas I wanted to start.
words.starter: The first one was …, whereas the second one
words.tutor: Give me two facts that are different from each other, and I will join them into one sentence with whereas.

words.meaning: Used when something happened even though there was a problem.
words.example: Despite the delay, we finished on the same day.
practice: Despite the rain, the market stayed open.
She passed, despite missing two weeks.
Despite the cost, it was worthwhile.
We got there on time, despite the roadworks.
words.tutor: Say a problem, then say what happened anyway, and I will join the two with despite.

words.meaning: Even so; that did not change what happened.
words.example: The room was cold. Nevertheless, everybody stayed.
practice: It was a long journey. Nevertheless, I would do it again.
The price went up. Nevertheless, we kept the booking.
She was tired; nevertheless, she finished the form.
The first try failed. Nevertheless, the second one worked.
words.tutor: Give me a problem in one sentence, and I will answer with a sentence that starts Nevertheless.

words.meaning: A word that adds one more point to the point before it.
words.example: The course was short. Furthermore, it was free.
practice: The room is warm. Furthermore, it is quiet.
The bus is cheap; furthermore, it stops outside.
Furthermore, the office is open on Saturday.
The tool is light. Furthermore, it is easy to clean.
words.tutor: Give me one good point about something, and I will add a second one starting with Furthermore.

words.meaning: When you look at the whole thing together.
words.example: Overall, the month went far better than I expected.
practice: Overall, it was a useful experience.
There were two bad days, but overall the week was fine.
Overall, I would say it was worthwhile.
How was it overall?
words.tutor: Tell me three things about your week, two good and one bad, and I will finish with one sentence starting Overall.

words.meaning: A person in your family, such as an aunt, a cousin or a brother.
words.example: A relative of mine drove me to the station.
practice: She stayed with a relative for two weeks.
Is he a relative, or a friend?
One relative came, and the rest sent a message.
I asked a relative to keep the key.
words.tutor: You may invent the family. Name three relatives and say what each one did, and I will ask you one question about each.

words.meaning: A person who saw something happen and can say what they saw.
words.example: A witness told the official what she had seen.
practice: There was one witness, and she was standing at the door.
The form asks for the name of a witness.
No witness saw the second car.
As a witness, you only say what you saw.
words.tutor: Describe a small event in three sentences, and I will ask you what a witness standing nearby would have seen.

words.meaning: A person whose job is to carry out the rules of an office or a service.
words.example: An official at the desk checked my form.
practice: The official asked for two documents.
A second official signed the card.
Which official do I give this to?
The official was polite, but the queue was long.
words.tutor: Ask me three questions that an official at a desk might ask, and I will answer each one in a full sentence.

words.meaning: A person whose job is to help another person at work.
words.example: The assistant found the file while I was waiting.
practice: Ask the assistant on the ground floor.
An assistant carried the boxes upstairs.
The assistant, whose desk is by the door, took the message.
She started as an assistant and learned quickly.
words.tutor: Give me a short problem at a counter, and I will write the line an assistant would say back to you.

words.meaning: A person who checks the work of other people and answers their questions.
words.example: My supervisor, whose office is upstairs, signed the record.
practice: The supervisor came round at four.
Ask the supervisor before you change the order.
A supervisor is not the same as an owner.
The supervisor was impressed by the second week.
words.tutor: Invent a job if you need one. Say one thing your supervisor checks, and I will ask you how often they check it.

words.meaning: A person who pays for a service, or who gets help from a service.
words.example: The client rang back the same afternoon.
practice: One client waited, whereas the other left.
The client, to whom I sent the card, replied at once.
We had three clients that morning.
A client is not always right, but always answered.
words.tutor: Invent a service. Tell me what your client wanted, and I will ask you what you said to them.

words.meaning: Something that has happened to you, and what it taught you.
words.example: The whole month was a useful experience.
practice: It was a hard experience, but I learned from it.
Have you ever had a similar experience?
She has experience of working at night.
My first experience of the new office was confusing.
words.starter: The best experience I have had is
words.tutor: Tell me about one experience in three sentences, and I will ask you what it taught you.

words.meaning: Something difficult that you did well.
words.example: Finishing the course was a real achievement.
practice: That was her biggest achievement of the year.
It is a small achievement, but it took months.
Write one achievement on the card.
The achievement was the team's, not mine alone.
words.starter: One achievement I am proud of is
words.tutor: Name one thing you finished that was difficult, and I will help you say it as one sentence about an achievement.

words.meaning: Something you remember from the past.
words.example: My clearest memory of that week is the queue.
practice: It is a good memory, despite the cold.
I have no memory of the second meeting.
That smell brings back a memory.
Her memory of the day is different from mine.
words.starter: One memory I still have is
words.tutor: Describe one memory in two sentences, and I will ask you one question about a detail you left out.

words.meaning: A sad feeling about something you did, or did not do.
words.example: My one regret is that I did not ask sooner.
practice: She left with no regret at all.
There is one regret in every long account.
His only regret was the wasted week.
Name one regret, then move on.
words.tutor: Tell me one thing you would do differently, and I will help you say it in one short sentence with regret.

words.meaning: A good thing that comes out of something.
words.example: The main benefit was the shorter journey.
practice: One benefit of the change is the quiet room.
There is no benefit in waiting until Friday.
The benefits were clear after a month.
Which benefit matters most to you?
words.tutor: Name a change you made, and I will ask you for two benefits and one problem it brought.

words.meaning: Something difficult that you have to deal with.
words.example: The biggest challenge was the first week.
practice: Learning the new system was a challenge.
Every challenge in that month had a solution.
It was a challenge, nevertheless we finished.
Name the challenge, then name what you did about it.
words.tutor: Tell me one difficult thing you are dealing with, and I will ask you what your first step would be.

words.meaning: It did what it was meant to do.
words.example: The second attempt was successful.
practice: It was a successful week overall.
Was the repair successful?
A successful plan is not always a quick one.
She has run a successful shop for six years.
words.tutor: Tell me about something you tried, and I will ask you whether it was successful and how you know.

words.meaning: It works well and gets the result you want.
words.example: A short list is more effective than a long one.
practice: The new method is far more effective.
Is this way effective, or only quick?
An effective answer is a short, clear, written one.
Cold water was not effective; hot water was.
words.starter: The most effective way to … is
words.tutor: Name two ways of doing the same job, and I will ask you which one is more effective and why.

words.meaning: Worth the time and the effort it took.
words.example: The extra hour was worthwhile.
practice: Despite the cost, the course was worthwhile.
Was the journey worthwhile?
It is worthwhile checking the form twice.
Nothing about that week was worthwhile.
words.tutor: Tell me something that took you a long time, and I will ask you whether it was worthwhile and what you got from it.

words.meaning: Not as good as you hoped.
words.example: The first meeting was disappointing.
practice: The result was disappointing, nevertheless we tried again.
It is disappointing to wait all day for nothing.
A disappointing start does not mean a disappointing month.
Why was the second week so disappointing?
words.tutor: Tell me about something that was not as good as you hoped, and I will ask you what would have made it better.

words.meaning: So good that people notice it.
words.example: The size of the building is impressive.
practice: That is an impressive amount of work for one week.
Her spoken English is impressive.
The old stone bridge is impressive at night.
It looked impressive, whereas it was quite simple.
words.tutor: Describe something you saw that people would notice, and I will ask you one question about why it is impressive.

words.meaning: It gives you a good feeling when it is finished.
words.example: Writing the last line was satisfying.
practice: It is satisfying to clear a whole shelf.
The most satisfying part was the end.
A satisfying job is not always an easy one.
She found the long, slow, careful work satisfying.
words.tutor: Name a job you finished recently, and I will ask you which part of it was the most satisfying.

grammar.title: While she was driving, I was reading the map
grammar.explanation: Sometimes two things went on at the same time. Both halves take was or were plus a verb with -ing. While goes in front of one of them. Neither action stops the other, and both take time. This is how you hold two people in one line of an account.
grammar.rule:
While plus was or were plus -ing, then was or were plus -ing.
While she was driving, I was reading the map.
While I was waiting at the desk, the assistant was looking for my file.
While the official was checking the form, my relative was parking the car.
Turn it round and the comma goes:
I was reading the map while she was driving.
You can use and instead of while:
She was driving and I was reading the map.
One long, one short is different. That one takes the past simple in the short half:
I was cooking when the power went off.
Question:
What were you doing while they were waiting?
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You want to say this: the two of you were both busy at the same moment.
Step 1. Name the two actions. She drove. I read the map.
Step 2. Ask whether both took time. Driving takes time. Reading a map takes time. Both do.
Step 3. So both halves get was or were plus -ing. She was driving. I was reading the map.
Step 4. Put while in front of one half. While she was driving.
Step 5. That half is first, so it needs a comma after it.
Answer: While she was driving, I was reading the map.
Now turn it round: I was reading the map while she was driving. No comma this time.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to write while she drove, I was reading. The while half needs was or were plus -ing too, because both actions are long. Write while she was driving. The other slip is using this pattern for a short action. If one thing happened in a second, it takes the past simple: I was waiting when the phone rang.
grammar.tip: Two long actions, two -ing verbs, one while.
grammar.practice:
Make one sentence from each pair. Put while in front of the first half. Both halves take was or were plus an -ing verb. Add a comma after the while half.
1. she drives / I read the map
2. I wait at the desk / the assistant looks for my file
3. the official checks the form / my relative parks the car
4. the supervisor talks to the client / I write the notes
5. they carry the boxes / we clean the floor
6. my brother cooks / the children play outside
7. the witness speaks / the second official listens
8. I fill in the card / the queue gets longer
grammar.answers:
1. While she was driving, I was reading the map.
2. While I was waiting at the desk, the assistant was looking for my file.
3. While the official was checking the form, my relative was parking the car.
4. While the supervisor was talking to the client, I was writing the notes.
5. While they were carrying the boxes, we were cleaning the floor.
6. While my brother was cooking, the children were playing outside.
7. While the witness was speaking, the second official was listening.
8. While I was filling in the card, the queue was getting longer.
The likeliest wrong answer is 1: writing while she drove. Both halves are long, so both need was or were plus -ing.
Item 8 catches people too. Getting longer is a slow change, not a sudden one, so it takes was getting.

grammar.title: Just finished, or ever in your life
grammar.explanation: Have or has plus the past form does two jobs here. One is what has only now happened, and the words for it are just and recently. The other is your whole life up to now, and the words for it are ever, never and before. Neither one names a date. If you name a date, the sentence goes back to the past simple.
grammar.rule:
Only now:
I have just finished the form.
She has just left the office.
They have recently moved the desks.
Just goes between have and the past form.
In your life, no date:
Have you ever done this before?
I have never been to that building.
I have done it twice.
Ask about it with ever, answer with never or a number.
Name a date and the sentence changes:
I finished the form at nine. Not: I have finished it at nine.
Recent, and still true:
She has been a supervisor since March.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You want to say this: you handed in the form two minutes ago.
Step 1. Ask whether you are naming a time. You are not. Two minutes ago is a feeling, not a date on the page.
Step 2. Ask which job it is. It happened only now, so this is the just job.
Step 3. Take have, because the subject is I.
Step 4. Put just straight after it. I have just.
Step 5. Add the past form of hand in. I have just handed in the form.
Answer: I have just handed in the form.
Now the other job. You are asking somebody about their whole life. Have you ever handed in a form like this?
grammar.mistake: It is easy to write I have finished the form at nine o'clock. Once you name the time, English wants the past simple: I finished the form at nine o'clock. The other slip is answering Have you ever with yesterday. Ever asks about your life, so the answer is yes I have, no I never have, or once, twice, three times.
grammar.tip: Just is a minute ago. Ever is your whole life. Neither one takes a date.
grammar.practice:
Write each sentence with have or has, and put just, recently, ever or never in the right place.
1. I (finish) the form. (a minute ago)
2. She (leave) the office. (a minute ago)
3. you (be) to this building? (in your life)
4. I (be) to this building. (not once in my life)
5. They (move) the desks. (in the last few weeks)
6. He (do) it twice. (in his life)
7. we (meet) the new client? (in our life)
8. The assistant (send) the card. (a minute ago)
grammar.answers:
1. I have just finished the form.
2. She has just left the office.
3. Have you ever been to this building?
4. I have never been to this building.
5. They have recently moved the desks.
6. He has done it twice.
7. Have we ever met the new client?
8. The assistant has just sent the card.
The likeliest wrong answer is 4: writing I have not ever been. That is not wrong, but never is the shorter and commoner form, and never already carries the not.
Item 3 catches people too. In a question, ever sits in front of the past form: Have you ever been?

grammar.title: Whose, whom, and the commas around extra detail
grammar.explanation: You already say the woman who fixed it. Whose means belonging to that person. Whom is used after a small word such as to, with or for. And when the detail is extra rather than necessary, it sits between two commas. Take the extra part out and the sentence must still make sense.
grammar.rule:
Whose, for belonging:
The assistant whose desk is by the door took the message.
My supervisor, whose office is upstairs, signed it.
Whom, after a small word:
The client to whom I sent the card replied at once.
The official with whom I spoke was very helpful.
Two commas, when the detail is extra:
My manager, who lives nearby, called me at seven.
Take it out: My manager called me at seven. Still a sentence.
No commas, when the detail says which one:
The official who signed it has left.
Take it out and you no longer know which official.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You want to say this: your supervisor signed it, and by the way their office is upstairs.
Step 1. Write the plain sentence first. My supervisor signed it on Friday.
Step 2. Name the extra detail. The office belongs to the supervisor.
Step 3. Belonging means whose. whose office is upstairs.
Step 4. Ask whether the detail is needed to know which person. You have only one supervisor, so it is not needed. It is extra.
Step 5. Extra means two commas, one at each end.
Answer: My supervisor, whose office is upstairs, signed it on Friday.
Check it. Take the part between the commas out: My supervisor signed it on Friday. Still a sentence, so the commas are right.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to write my supervisor, who's office is upstairs. Who's is short for who is, and an office cannot be who is. Belonging takes whose, with no mark in it. The other slip is one comma instead of two. If you open with a comma you must close with one: My manager, who lives nearby, called.
grammar.practice:
Join each pair into one sentence. Use whose or whom. Add two commas where the detail is extra, and none where it says which one.
1. My supervisor signed it. Her office is upstairs. (extra)
2. The client replied at once. I sent the card to him. (extra)
3. The assistant took the message. Her desk is by the door. (says which one)
4. My relative drove me. His car is very old. (extra)
5. The official has left. I spoke with her. (says which one)
6. The witness gave a statement. Her name is on the form. (extra)
7. The supervisor asked for it. I work with him. (says which one)
8. A neighbour helped us. Her son is a driver. (extra)
grammar.answers:
1. My supervisor, whose office is upstairs, signed it.
2. The client, to whom I sent the card, replied at once.
3. The assistant whose desk is by the door took the message.
4. My relative, whose car is very old, drove me.
5. The official with whom I spoke has left.
6. The witness, whose name is on the form, gave a statement.
7. The supervisor with whom I work asked for it.
8. A neighbour, whose son is a driver, helped us.
The likeliest wrong answer is 2: leaving the small word out and writing the client whom I sent the card. Whom needs its small word in front: to whom.
Item 3 catches people too. It says which assistant, so it takes no commas at all.
grammar.tip: Whose is belonging. Whom follows a small word. Extra detail wears two commas.

grammar.title: An impressive old leather chair: three in a row
grammar.explanation: You already know size, then age, then material. Now put three in a row, and start with what you think of it. The order is opinion, size, age, colour, material. One of the three may end in -ing or -ed, and it behaves like any other describing word. No commas are needed in this order, and no and either.
grammar.rule:
Opinion, size, age, colour, material. Pick three.
an impressive old leather chair
a useful small plastic box
a disappointing long grey queue
a satisfying short walk home
With an -ing or -ed one among them:
a tiring three-hour meeting
an interesting old printed form
a finished wooden shelf
The -ing one is about the thing. The -ed one is about the person:
It was a tiring day. I was tired.
Three with commas is a different thing. Use commas when all three are opinions:
a long, slow, careful piece of work
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You want to describe a chair. It is old. It is leather. You think it is impressive.
Step 1. Sort the three words. Impressive is your opinion. Old is age. Leather is material.
Step 2. Put them in the order: opinion, then age, then material.
Step 3. impressive, then old, then leather.
Step 4. No commas, because they are different kinds.
Step 5. Add a or an. The first sound is a vowel sound, so it is an.
Answer: an impressive old leather chair.
Now one with an -ed word: an interesting old printed form. Interesting is the opinion, old is age, printed is how it was made.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to write a leather old impressive chair. English puts your opinion first and the material last. The other slip is a comma between every word: an impressive, old, leather chair. Commas belong there only when all three words are opinions, as in a long, slow, careful piece of work.
grammar.tip: What you think, then how big, how old, what colour, what it is made of.
grammar.practice:
Put the words in the right order in front of the noun. Add a or an.
1. leather / old / impressive / chair
2. plastic / small / useful / box
3. grey / long / disappointing / queue
4. printed / old / interesting / form
5. metal / new / effective / tool
6. wooden / narrow / satisfying / shelf
7. cotton / white / clean / towel
8. three-hour / tiring / meeting
grammar.answers:
1. an impressive old leather chair
2. a useful small plastic box
3. a disappointing long grey queue
4. an interesting old printed form
5. an effective new metal tool
6. a satisfying narrow wooden shelf
7. a clean white cotton towel
8. a tiring three-hour meeting
The likeliest wrong answer is 1: writing a leather old impressive chair. Material always comes last and opinion always comes first.
Item 4 catches people too. Printed looks like a verb, but here it describes the form, so it sits with the other describing words.

grammar.title: Far better, much worse: making a comparison stronger
grammar.explanation: Better and worse are already comparisons. Far, much and a lot make them stronger. They go in front of the comparing word, never in front of the plain word. A bit and slightly work the same way and make it weaker. Well is the odd one: the comparing form of well is better, not weller.
grammar.rule:
Stronger:
It went far better than I expected.
It took much longer than the notice said.
The second week was a lot busier.
Weaker:
It was a bit worse than last time.
She finished slightly earlier.
With a long word, the much goes in front of more:
It is much more effective than the old way.
With the way something is done:
They dealt with it far more quickly this time.
Well becomes better, and badly becomes worse:
I did it well. I did it much better the second time.
Never: much good, much quick.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You want to say this: the month went well, and better than you thought it would.
Step 1. Start with the plain comparison. It went better than I expected.
Step 2. Ask how much better. A long way better.
Step 3. That means far, much or a lot.
Step 4. Put it straight in front of the comparing word, not in front of well.
Step 5. far better, not far well.
Answer: It went far better than I expected.
Now a long word: effective becomes more effective, so the strengthener sits in front of more. It is much more effective than the old way.
grammar.mistake: It is easy to write it went much good. Much needs a comparing word after it, so write much better. The other slip is very in this job: very better is not English. Very belongs in front of the plain word, as in very good, and far, much and a lot belong in front of the comparing one.
grammar.tip: Far, much and a lot need a comparing word behind them. Never much good.
grammar.practice:
Make each comparison stronger with far, much or a lot. Use the comparing form of the word in brackets.
1. It went (well) than I expected.
2. It took (long) than the notice said.
3. The second week was (busy) than the first.
4. This way is (effective) than the old way.
5. They dealt with it (quickly) this time.
6. The queue was (bad) on Monday.
7. The new room is (quiet) than the old one.
8. She speaks (confidently) than she did in March.
grammar.answers:
1. It went far better than I expected.
2. It took much longer than the notice said.
3. The second week was a lot busier than the first.
4. This way is much more effective than the old way.
5. They dealt with it far more quickly this time.
6. The queue was much worse on Monday.
7. The new room is far quieter than the old one.
8. She speaks much more confidently than she did in March.
Any of far, much and a lot is right in items 1 to 3 and 6 to 8. The comparing form is what is being checked.
The likeliest wrong answer is 1: writing far well. Well has its own comparing form, and it is better.
Item 5 catches people too. Quickly is about the way, so it becomes more quickly, and the strengthener goes in front of more.

readings.title: The month the office moved
readings.setting: A workplace and a new building across the road
readings.passage:
Here is the background. Our office moved across the road in March. The new building was ready, whereas the old one was not safe any more.

The first week was the hardest. While the two drivers were carrying the boxes down, we were cleaning the floor upstairs. Nobody had a desk of their own. My supervisor, whose office is now on the third floor, spent the whole week standing up with a list in her hand.

Then the phones stopped working. The client to whom I had sent the new number rang the old one instead, and got nothing at all. That was the low point. It was a long, slow, disappointing Tuesday.

The assistant whose desk is by the door saved us. She wrote the new number on a large white card and put it in the window. Despite the lost morning, we answered every call by four o'clock.

The second week was much better. We had recently learned where everything was, and the new room is far quieter than the old one. Furthermore, the bus stops outside the door.

Looking back, the biggest challenge was not the boxes. It was telling two hundred people where we had gone. The main benefit is the short journey. My one regret is that I did not write the new number on the card in January.

I have just finished the report about the move. I have never written one that long before. Overall, the month went far better than I expected, and it was a useful experience. It was not a comfortable one, nevertheless I would do it again.

readings.title: How to tell the whole story
readings.setting: A page from a self-study writing guide
readings.passage:
A short account tells one moment. A whole account tells something that took time: a month, a course, a repair, a move. It has four parts, and they always come in the same order.

Part one is the background. Say what a person needs to know before the story starts. Two sentences are usually enough. A reader who does not have the background will stop and ask a question instead of reading on.

Part two is what happened. Keep it in order. Use time words to carry the reader forward: first, then, after that, by the end. Where two things happened at once, say so with while. While the drivers were carrying the boxes, we were cleaning the floor.

Part three is the people. Name them by what they do: the assistant, the supervisor, the official, the client, a relative, a witness. Add one piece of extra detail about each one, between two commas. My supervisor, whose office is upstairs, kept the list.

Part four is what you made of it. This is the part most writers leave out, and it is the part a reader remembers. Name the challenge. Name the benefit. Name one regret. Then judge the whole thing in one line, starting with overall.

Four joining words do most of the work. Whereas puts two different facts side by side. Despite says that something happened even though there was a problem. Nevertheless says that a problem did not change the ending. Furthermore adds one more point.

In my view the fourth part is worth more than the other three together. A list of events is a timetable. An account with a judgement in it is a story.

readings.title: End-of-course record card
readings.setting: A card handed out at the end of an adult English course
readings.passage:
ADULT ENGLISH COURSE: END-OF-COURSE RECORD CARD

PART A. THE LEARNER FILLS THIS IN
Name: Lena
Course: Adult English, evening group
Started: 4 March. Finished: 26 June.
Hours attended: 58 of 64.

PART B. FOUR RESULTS, ONE LINE EACH
Listening: 7 of 9.
Reading: 8 of 10.
Speaking: 4 of 5.
Writing: 5 of 6.
Do not add these four numbers together. One total would hide the skill that needs more time.

PART C. ONE ACHIEVEMENT AND ONE CHALLENGE
Achievement: I have spoken on the phone in English three times.
Challenge: writing the past forms of irregular verbs.

PART D. THE SUPERVISOR OR COURSE OFFICIAL SIGNS HERE
Signed by the supervisor whose name is printed below.
Name of official: Nadia. Date: 26 June.

PART E. ASKING FOR A REFERENCE
A reference is a short written note about your work. You may ask for one up to twelve months after the last day.
1. Write to the office. Give your name, the course and the two dates.
2. Say who the reference is for, and by which date you need it.
3. Allow ten working days. Do not ring before the ten days have passed.
4. Keep this card. The office cannot write a reference without the dates on it.

PART F. NOTES
A record card is not a certificate. The certificate is posted separately.
This card is an example. The parts are different on every course.

comprehension.q: What were the two drivers doing while the writer was cleaning the floor?
comprehension.a: They were carrying the boxes down.
comprehension.why: The first-week paragraph puts the two actions side by side with while, so both were going on at the same time.

comprehension.q: Why did the client ring a number that gave no answer?
comprehension.a: The phones had stopped working, and the client rang the old number instead of the new one.
comprehension.why: The third paragraph says the client rang the old number and got nothing at all.

comprehension.q: The writer says the new room is far quieter than the old one. What does far do to the word quieter?
comprehension.why: Far, much and a lot sit in front of a comparing word and say that the difference is big. Quieter on its own would be a smaller difference.

comprehension.q: The writer's one regret is about the card in the window. What does that tell you they think went wrong?
comprehension.a: They think the new number should have been shown to people much earlier.
comprehension.why: The card fixed the problem in one afternoon, so wishing it had been written in January means the fix was simple and came too late.

comprehension.q: Overall, does the writer think the month was worthwhile? Give the words that show it.
comprehension.a: Yes. The last paragraph says it went far better than I expected and I would do it again.
comprehension.why: Overall marks the writer's judgement of the whole month, and the last line accepts the discomfort and still says yes.

comprehension.q: Which of the four parts of an account does the page say most writers leave out?
comprehension.a: Part four, what you made of it.
comprehension.why: The fourth paragraph says it is the part most writers leave out and the part a reader remembers.

comprehension.q: According to the page, what job does whereas do in a sentence?
comprehension.a: It puts two different facts side by side.
comprehension.why: The joining-words paragraph gives that meaning for whereas, and a different one for despite.

comprehension.q: The writer says an account with a judgement in it is a story, and a list of events is a timetable. What is their opinion?
comprehension.a: That the judgement matters more than the list of events.
comprehension.why: The last paragraph opens with in my view, which marks an opinion, and then says part four is worth more than the other three together.

comprehension.q: You want a reference from this course. How long must you wait before you ring the office?
comprehension.why: Part E, step 3 says allow ten working days and do not ring before they have passed.

comprehension.q: You have lost the card and you want a reference. Why is that a problem, and what must you find?
comprehension.a: The office cannot write a reference without the dates, so you must find the date you started and the date you finished.
comprehension.why: Part E asks for your name, the course and the two dates. Its last line says the office cannot write the reference without them.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Two things at once
speaking.instructions:
Say these eight lines out loud. Then record them and play them back.
While she was driving, I was reading the map.
While I was waiting at the desk, the assistant was looking for my file.
While the official was checking the form, my relative was parking the car.
While the supervisor was talking to the client, I was writing the notes.
While they were carrying the boxes, we were cleaning the floor.
I was filling in the card while the queue was getting longer.
What were you doing while they were waiting?
While the witness was speaking, the second official was listening.
Now make six of your own about one busy morning. You may invent every detail.
Play your recording back.
Check one thing only: count the -ing verbs in each sentence.
Two -ing verbs is right. One means the while half slipped into the past simple.
speaking.tutor: Give me six half sentences that start with while, and I will finish each one with a second long action.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Just now, and ever in my life
speaking.instructions:
Say these lines out loud, then record them.
I have just finished the form.
She has just left the office.
They have recently moved the desks.
Have you ever been to this building?
I have never been to this building.
I have done it twice.
Have we ever met this client?
The assistant has just sent the card.
Now say six of your own. Three with just or recently, three with ever or never. You may invent all six.
Play the recording back.
Check one thing only: listen for a date or a clock time.
If you hear yesterday, at nine or last week, that sentence needs the past simple instead.
Say it again the other way and move on.
speaking.tutor: Ask me six questions starting Have you ever, and I will answer each one. Tell me if I ever put a date in the answer.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Three words before the thing
speaking.instructions:
Look at eight things around you, or invent eight. Describe each one with three describing words.
Say them in this order: what you think of it, then how big or how old, then what it is made of.
Model lines:
It is an impressive old leather chair.
It is a useful small plastic box.
It is a satisfying narrow wooden shelf.
It is a clean white cotton towel.
It was a tiring three-hour meeting.
It is an interesting old printed form.
Record all eight and play them back.
Check one thing only: count the describing words in each line.
Three is right. If your opinion word is not first, say that line again.
speaking.tutor: Name a thing, and I will give you three describing words in the wrong order. Put them in the right order and I will tell you if it is correct.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — How did it go?
speaking.instructions:
This is a conversation. Say both halves out loud, then record the whole thing.
A: How did the second week go?
B: Far better than I expected.
A: Did it take long?
B: Much longer than the notice said.
A: Is the new way any good?
B: It is much more effective than the old way.
A: And the queue?
B: A lot worse on Monday, whereas Friday was fine.
A: Was it worthwhile?
B: Overall, yes. It was a useful experience.
A: Any regret?
B: One. I did not ask sooner.
Now change every B answer to your own. You may invent the week.
Play it back and check one thing: after far, much and a lot there must be a comparing word.
Far better is right. Far good is not.
If somebody is with you, take part A and let them answer. Doing it alone works the same way.
speaking.tutor: Ask me the six A questions one at a time, and I will answer each one with far, much or a lot. Tell me if any answer is missing the comparing word.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Listen, then pass it on
speaking.instructions:
Use the Listen button on the second reading, How to tell the whole story.
Listen once with the page covered. Do not write.
Listen a second time and write four short notes: three facts and one opinion.
A fact is something the page states. An opinion is what the writer thinks.
Now record yourself passing it on in about one minute.
Use these three shapes:
The page says that an account has four parts.
It says that the background comes first.
In the writer's view, the judgement matters more than the list of events.
Play your recording back with the page open in front of you.
Check three things you can see: did you give three facts, did you give one opinion, and did you keep them apart?
A fact said as an opinion, or an opinion said as a fact, counts as missed.
speaking.tutor: I will say four short statements about a course. Tell me which of them are facts and which one is an opinion, and say how you knew.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — The A2 check: the speaking half
speaking.instructions:
This is one of the four parts of the level check. Record once, for about one minute.
Tell the whole story of something that took time. A month, a course, a repair, a move. You may invent all of it.
Say these five things, in this order:
1. The background, in two sentences.
2. What happened, with one while sentence holding two long actions.
3. One person in it, with extra detail between two commas.
4. The challenge and the benefit.
5. Your judgement, in one sentence starting with overall.
Play it back once and tick the five points you can hear. Pauses and restarts are fine and do not cost a point.
Write your result as one line: Speaking, and the number out of 5.
Keep the recording. It goes in the portfolio.
speaking.tutor: I will read you the five points one at a time. Say your sentence for each, and I will tell you whether it does what the point asks.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Two things just now, two things ever
writing.prompt: Write four sentences about yourself. Two say what has only now happened. Two say what you have, or have never, done in your life. You may invent every detail. Do not put a date in any of the four.
writing.model:
I have just finished a long form for the office.
I have recently moved to a quieter room.
I have never spoken on the phone in English.
Have you ever waited a whole morning for one signature?
writing.criteria: Four sentences. Every sentence uses have or has plus a past form. Two use just or recently. Two use ever or never. No sentence names a date or a clock time.
writing.support: Do one in two steps. Write the plain past sentence first: I finished a long form. Then change it: take out any time word, put have in front and just after it. I have just finished a long form.
writing.extension: Add a fifth sentence naming a date, in the past simple, and put it beside one of your have sentences so you can see the difference.

writing.title: Writing 2 — The people in the account
writing.prompt: Write four sentences about four people in one account. Use a supervisor, an assistant, a client and a relative, or invent four others. Give each one a piece of extra detail with whose or whom, between two commas.
writing.model:
My supervisor, whose office is upstairs, signed the record on Friday.
The assistant, whose desk is by the door, wrote the number on a card.
The client, to whom I sent the new number, rang back the same afternoon.
My relative, whose car is very old, drove me to the office at seven.
writing.criteria: Four sentences. Each one names a person and adds extra detail. Each has a comma at both ends of the extra part. Take the part between the commas out and each sentence still makes sense.
writing.support: Write the plain sentence on its own line first: My supervisor signed the record. Then write the extra detail on a second line: whose office is upstairs. Only then push the second line into the middle of the first, with a comma at each end.
writing.extension: Add a fifth sentence where the detail says which person you mean. That one takes no commas at all.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Background, what happened, what I made of it
writing.prompt:
Plan and write a connected account in three paragraphs. Choose something that took time: a month, a course, a repair, a move, a long wait. You may invent all of it.
Plan first, on four lines: the background, two events in order, one person, one judgement.
Then write the three paragraphs under a heading of your own.
writing.model:
Learning to use the new booking system

Here is the background. The office changed its booking system in April. The old one was slow, whereas the new one does the same job in two steps.

The first week was the challenge. While the supervisor was showing us the screens, the phones were ringing all morning. The assistant, whose desk is nearest the door, took most of the calls. Despite the noise, we had all learned the six steps by Friday.

Overall, the change was worthwhile. The main benefit is the shorter booking. My one regret is that I did not write the steps down on the first day. It was a tiring, confusing, useful week, and I would say the new system is far more effective than the old one.
writing.length: Three paragraphs, four to six sentences each
writing.criteria: A heading on its own line. Three paragraphs with a blank line between them. Paragraph one gives the background. Paragraph two tells what happened, with one while sentence and one person described between two commas. Paragraph three starts with overall and names one benefit and one regret. At least two of these words appear: whereas, despite, nevertheless, furthermore.
writing.support: Write the plan first and nothing else. Four lines, four short notes. Then turn line one into paragraph one, lines two into paragraph two, and lines three and four into paragraph three. A paragraph is easier to write from a note than from nothing.
writing.extension: Add a fourth paragraph of two sentences that says what you would do differently next time, and start it with nevertheless.

writing.title: Writing 4 — The A2 check: the writing half
writing.prompt:
This is one of the four parts of the level check. Write it by hand, on paper, not on a screen. Writing by hand at a steady speed is part of what is being checked here.
Write one connected account of about 120 words about something that took time. You may invent all of it. Use the shape from Writing 3, but write it in one go, without a plan in front of you.
writing.model:
The month the office moved

Here is the background. Our office moved across the road in March. The new building was ready, whereas the old one was not safe any more. While the drivers were carrying the boxes down, we were cleaning the floor upstairs. My supervisor, whose office is now on the third floor, kept the whole list in her hand. The phones stopped for a morning. Despite that, we answered every call by four. The biggest challenge was telling people where we had gone. The main benefit is the short journey. I have just finished the report about it. Overall, the month went far better than I expected.
writing.length: About 120 words, handwritten, in three paragraphs
writing.criteria: Six points, one mark each. 1. A heading and three paragraphs. 2. One while sentence with two -ing verbs. 3. One have or has sentence with just, recently, ever or never. 4. One person with extra detail between two commas. 5. Three describing words in a row somewhere. 6. A last sentence starting with overall, with far, much or a lot in it. Read your own writing back and tick only what you can point at.
writing.support: If the blank page is the problem, copy the six points down the side of your paper first. Write one sentence for each point, in order, and join them afterwards. Six sentences joined is already an account.
writing.extension: Read it aloud and record it. That recording can serve as the speaking half of the portfolio if your first one was rushed.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Which word?
activities.instructions:
Write one word in each gap.
Use: background, whereas, despite, nevertheless, overall, witness, supervisor, client, achievement, regret, benefit, challenge.
1. A person who saw it happen is a ____ .
2. A person who pays for a service is a ____ .
3. A person who checks the work of others is a ____ .
4. What a reader needs to know before the story starts is the ____ .
5. Something difficult that you did well is an ____ .
6. A good thing that comes out of something is a ____ .
7. Something difficult you have to deal with is a ____ .
8. A sad feeling about what you did not do is a ____ .
9. The word that puts two different facts side by side is ____ .
10. The word that means it happened even though there was a problem is ____ .
11. The word that means a problem did not change the ending is ____ .
12. The word for looking at the whole thing together is ____ .
activities.answers:
1. witness 2. client 3. supervisor 4. background 5. achievement 6. benefit 7. challenge 8. regret 9. whereas 10. despite 11. nevertheless 12. overall
Twelve of twelve: move on. Nine to eleven: read the word cards for the ones you missed. Eight or fewer: read all four groups again, then do this once more.
activities.solo: Cover the word list with your hand for the first six items. Uncover it only when you are stuck, and mark which ones needed it.

activities.title: Practice 2 — At the same time, or one after the other
activities.instructions:
Choose the right form for the words in brackets. Two long actions take was or were plus -ing in both halves. One long and one short takes the past simple in the short half.
1. While she (drive), I (read) the map.
2. I (wait) at the desk when the phone (ring).
3. While they (carry) the boxes, we (clean) the floor.
4. He (cook) when the power (go) off.
5. While the official (check) the form, my relative (park) the car.
6. She (write) the card while the queue (get) longer.
7. I (stand) at the window when the bus (arrive).
8. While the supervisor (talk) to the client, the assistant (answer) the phone.
activities.answers:
1. While she was driving, I was reading the map.
2. I was waiting at the desk when the phone rang.
3. While they were carrying the boxes, we were cleaning the floor.
4. He was cooking when the power went off.
5. While the official was checking the form, my relative was parking the car.
6. She was writing the card while the queue was getting longer.
7. I was standing at the window when the bus arrived.
8. While the supervisor was talking to the client, the assistant was answering the phone.
Eight of eight: move on. Six or seven: look again at the four items with when in them. Five or fewer: read grammar card 1 again and redo all eight.
The test is simple. While takes two -ing verbs. When usually takes one -ing verb and one short past form.
activities.solo: Mark each item W or N before you write anything: W for while, N for when. Do the eight forms only after all eight letters are on the page.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Just, recently, ever, never
activities.instructions:
Put just, recently, ever or never in each sentence. One sentence needs none of them, because it names a time.
1. I have ____ finished the form. (a minute ago)
2. Have you ____ been to this building? (in your life)
3. I have ____ been to this building. (not once)
4. They have ____ moved the desks. (in the last few weeks)
5. She has ____ left the office. (a minute ago)
6. I finished the form at nine o'clock. (a named time)
7. Have we ____ met this client? (in our life)
8. The assistant has ____ sent the card. (a minute ago)
activities.answers:
1. just 2. ever 3. never 4. recently 5. just 6. none of them; the sentence is already right, because at nine o'clock names a time and takes the past simple 7. ever 8. just
Eight of eight: move on. Six or seven: read the rule lines on grammar card 2 again. Five or fewer: redo the card practice first, then come back.
Item 6 is the one that decides whether you have understood. A named time closes the door on have and has.
activities.solo: Before you answer, write A or B beside each item: A for a minute ago, B for in your life. Item 6 gets neither letter, and that is the answer.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Whose, whom, and the commas
activities.instructions:
Write whose or whom in each gap, then add the commas where the detail is extra. Four of the eight need two commas. Four need none.
1. My supervisor ____ office is upstairs signed it. (extra)
2. The assistant ____ desk is by the door took the message. (says which one)
3. The client to ____ I sent the card replied at once. (extra)
4. The official with ____ I spoke has left. (says which one)
5. My relative ____ car is very old drove me. (extra)
6. The witness ____ name is on the form gave a statement. (extra)
7. The supervisor with ____ I work asked for it. (says which one)
8. The neighbour ____ son is a driver keeps our key. (says which one)
activities.answers:
1. My supervisor, whose office is upstairs, signed it.
2. The assistant whose desk is by the door took the message.
3. The client, to whom I sent the card, replied at once.
4. The official with whom I spoke has left.
5. My relative, whose car is very old, drove me.
6. The witness, whose name is on the form, gave a statement.
7. The supervisor with whom I work asked for it.
8. The neighbour whose son is a driver keeps our key.
Eight of eight: move on. Six or seven: check the four that need commas. Five or fewer: read grammar card 3 again and redo all eight.
Whose comes straight in front of a thing that belongs to the person. Whom always has a small word such as to or with in front of it.
activities.solo: Test every comma yourself. Cover the words between your two commas with a finger. If what is left is still a sentence, the commas are right.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Three in order, then a stronger comparison
activities.instructions:
Part 1. Put the describing words in the right order and add a or an.
1. leather / old / impressive / chair
2. plastic / small / useful / box
3. printed / old / interesting / form
4. metal / new / effective / tool
Part 2. Write the comparison with far, much or a lot, and the comparing form of the word in brackets.
5. It went ____ (well) than I expected.
6. The queue was ____ (bad) on Monday.
7. This way is ____ (effective) than the old way.
8. They dealt with it ____ (quickly) this time.
activities.answers:
1. an impressive old leather chair
2. a useful small plastic box
3. an interesting old printed form
4. an effective new metal tool
5. It went far better than I expected.
6. The queue was much worse on Monday.
7. This way is much more effective than the old way.
8. They dealt with it far more quickly this time.
Any of far, much and a lot is right in 5 to 8. The comparing form is what is being checked.
Eight of eight: move on. Six or seven: check whether your opinion word came first in Part 1. Five or fewer: read grammar cards 4 and 5 again and redo this.
Items 5 and 6 are the traps. Well becomes better, and bad becomes worse, so far well and much bad are both wrong.
activities.solo: In Part 1, label each word before you write the line: O for opinion, S for size, A for age, M for material. The letters go in that order, and the words follow them.

activities.title: Practice 6 — The A2 check: the listening half
activities.instructions:
Use the Listen button on the first reading, The month the office moved. Cover the page with a sheet of paper.
Listen once without writing. Then listen again and answer these nine questions from what you heard.
1. In which month did the office move?
2. What were the two drivers doing while the writer was cleaning the floor?
3. Where is the supervisor's office now?
4. What stopped working?
5. What did the assistant write the new number on?
6. By what time were all the calls answered?
7. What does the writer say is the main benefit?
8. What is the writer's one regret?
9. Overall, was the month better or worse than the writer expected?
Uncover the page only after all nine answers are written.
activities.answers:
1. March. 2. Carrying the boxes down. 3. On the third floor. 4. The phones. 5. A large white card. 6. Four o'clock. 7. The short journey. 8. Not writing the new number on the card in January. 9. Far better than expected.
Questions 1 to 6 are detail. Questions 7 to 9 are what the speaker made of it, which is the harder half.
Write your result as one line: Listening, and the number out of 9.
Seven or more of nine is a secure A2 in listening. Five or six means listen once more each time before you answer. Four or fewer means use the page and the audio together for a while.
activities.solo: Do not read the page while the audio is playing, even once. Reading and listening at the same time measures your reading, and you already measure that in the comprehension questions.

quizzes.q: Which sentence has two long actions going on at the same time?
options: While she was driving, I was reading the map.
I was cooking when the power went off.
She drove and then I read the map.
I read the map after she stopped the car.
quizzes.a: While she was driving, I was reading the map.
quizzes.why: Both halves have was plus an -ing verb, so both actions take time and run together. The cooking one is the tempting choice, because it also has an -ing verb, but went off is a single moment cutting across the cooking. The other two put the actions one after the other.

quizzes.q: You handed the form in one minute ago. Which sentence is right?
options: I have finished the form at nine o'clock.
I have just finished the form.
I have ever finished the form.
I finish the form just now.
quizzes.a: I have just finished the form.
quizzes.why: Just goes between have and the past form and means only now. The first option is the tempting one, and it looks the same until you see at nine o'clock. A named time sends the sentence back to the past simple. Ever asks about your whole life, and the last option uses the wrong verb form.

quizzes.q: Which sentence punctuates the extra detail correctly?
options: My supervisor whose office is upstairs, signed it.
My supervisor, who's office is upstairs, signed it.
My supervisor, whose office is upstairs, signed it.
My supervisor, whose office is upstairs signed it.
quizzes.a: My supervisor, whose office is upstairs, signed it.
quizzes.why: Extra detail needs a comma at each end, and belonging takes whose. The second option is the tempting one, because who's sounds the same; it is short for who is, and an office cannot be who is. The other two open the commas and never close them, or close them and never open them.

options: a leather old impressive chair
an old impressive leather chair
a leather impressive old chair
an impressive old leather chair
quizzes.why: The order is what you think of it, then how old, then what it is made of. The second option is the tempting one, because old and leather are in the right order and only the opinion word is out of place. Your opinion always comes first.

quizzes.q: Which sentence makes the comparison stronger, and is correct English?
options: It went far better than I expected.
It went much good.
It went very better than I expected.
It went far well than I expected.
quizzes.a: It went far better than I expected.
quizzes.why: Far, much and a lot must be followed by a comparing word, and the comparing form of well is better. Much good fails because good is the plain form. Very better fails because very belongs in front of a plain word. Far well fails because well has its own comparing form.

quizzes.q: The first week was quiet, ____ the second was very busy. Which word fits?
options: despite
whereas
furthermore
nevertheless
quizzes.why: Whereas puts two different facts side by side, which is exactly what the two halves are. Despite is the tempting one, but it needs a noun after it, not a whole sentence. Furthermore adds a point that agrees, and nevertheless says a problem did not change the ending.

quizzes.q: From Unit 15. Which sentence says what somebody's job is?
options: She looks like a nurse.
She deals with a nurse.
She works as a nurse.
She looks after a nurse.
quizzes.why: As names the job the person actually does. Looks like is the tempting one, because it is only one word different; like compares her appearance to a nurse and says nothing about her job. Deals with and looks after describe what she does to somebody else.

quizzes.q: From Unit 16. The parcel arrived yesterday. Which sentence says so without naming who brought it?
options: Somebody delivered the parcel yesterday.
The parcel is delivered yesterday.
The parcel delivered yesterday.
The parcel was delivered yesterday.
quizzes.why: Was plus the past form puts the parcel first and leaves the deliverer out. The first option is the tempting one, because it also hides the name, but somebody is still doing the action in the sentence. The second uses the present for a past day, and the third leaves the was out altogether.

quizzes.q: From Unit 17. The supervisor said these words: wait here. Which sentence passes them on?
options: She told me to wait there.
She said me to wait there.
She told to wait there.
She said me that wait there.
quizzes.a: She told me to wait there.
quizzes.why: Tell takes a person straight after it, and an instruction passed on takes to plus the verb. The second option is the tempting one, because it is otherwise perfect. Say never takes a person after it, so it would have to be she said that I should wait. The third drops the person that tell needs.

quizzes.q: From Unit 18. Which sentence is right?
options: When the parcel will come, I will ring you.
When the parcel comes, I will ring you.
When the parcel comes, I ring you.
When the parcel will come, I ring you.
quizzes.a: When the parcel comes, I will ring you.
quizzes.why: The time half stays in the present and the other half takes will. The first option is the tempting one, because both halves really are about the future. English still keeps will out of the half that begins with when, until, before or as soon as. The third drops the will from the half that needs it.

quizzes.q: From Unit 19. Your neighbour asks what to do about a broken lock. Which sentence gives advice?
options: You must ring the office today.
You needn't ring the office today.
You should ring the office today.
You are ringing the office today.
quizzes.a: You should ring the office today.
quizzes.why: Should offers advice and leaves the choice with the other person. Must is the tempting one, but it says the person has no choice, which is not advice. Needn't says the opposite of what is meant, and the last option describes an arrangement rather than advising anything.

quizzes.q: From Unit 8. You started the job in March and you are still doing it. Which sentence is right?
options: I work here since March.
I have worked here for March.
I worked here since March.
I have worked here since March.
quizzes.a: I have worked here since March.
quizzes.why: Since names the starting point, and have worked says it is still true today. The second option is the tempting one, because it has the right verb form. For needs a length of time, such as for four months, not a starting point. The other two use the wrong verb form for something that is still true.

teacherNotes.note: The while half slipping into the past simple is the error that lasts longest here, and repeating the rule rarely fixes it, because the learner already agrees with the rule. What fixes it is a counting habit: read the sentence out loud and count the -ing verbs. A while sentence has two. A when sentence usually has one, and the short action beside it is a single past form. Practice 2 is built for exactly that, and two runs of it usually settles the pattern.

Three of the five cards are increments on patterns from earlier in the level, and a learner who stumbles is usually stumbling on the earlier half. Unit 3 taught have plus a past form with no stated time, and Unit 8 taught for and since. Unit 20 adds only just and recently for what has only now happened, and ever and never for a whole life. Unit 9 taught size, age and material, and the -ing and -ed pair. Unit 20 adds only the opinion word at the front and three in a row. If the new half is not landing, go back to the earlier unit's card for ten minutes rather than repeating this one.

The check produces four numbers and they must stay four numbers: listening out of 9, reading out of 10, speaking out of 5, writing out of 6. Adding them together produces a single figure that looks like a grade and hides the skill that needs the time. The commonest shape at this point is strong reading and weak speaking, and a total of 24 out of 30 conceals that completely. Record the four on four lines, and read the lowest one as the answer to what to do next.

The account in the first reading, the record card and every person named in this unit are examples, not advice. Reference rules, course records and signatures differ from place to place, and this unit cannot say what would happen in any particular case. What it can give is the English needed to ask. Every task here may be answered with an invented job, an invented week, an invented family and an invented name, and the last reading says on its own last line that it is an example.

The portfolio is marked on all eight rubric criteria, four marks each. The temptation is to mark the newest work hardest, but the point of the portfolio is the distance travelled across the level, so a Unit 15 piece is judged against Unit 15 and not against Unit 20. Count three visible things before judging anything else: four units represented, two recordings present, and one written account of about 120 words. A portfolio missing any of those three is incomplete rather than weak.

selfAssessment.statement: I can say what two people were doing at the same time.
I can write what I have just done and what I have never done.
I can add extra detail about a person between two commas.
I can describe a thing with three describing words in the right order.
I can say that one thing was far better or much worse than another.
I can plan and write a long account by hand, in paragraphs.
I can listen to a long account and say what the speaker thought of it.
I can read a long text and say what it is mainly about.

assignment.title: The level portfolio, and the A2 check in four skills
assignment.instructions:
This is the last piece of work in the level. It has three parts. You may invent every detail in all of them.

PART 1. THE PORTFOLIO: FOUR UNITS AND TWO RECORDINGS
Gather work you have already done. Choose four of these five units, and take one piece from each.
Unit 15: one question you asked to open a subject up, written out with the answer.
Unit 16: three sentences saying how something is made, without naming who makes it.
Unit 17: one thing somebody told you, passed on with said or told.
Unit 18: one plan, and what you will do if it goes wrong.
Unit 19: one piece of advice you would give, with should or ought to.
Then add two recordings: Speaking 4 from this unit, and Speaking 6.
On the front, write a card of six lines: your name or an invented one, the four units you chose, the date, one achievement, one challenge, and one line starting Overall.

PART 2. THE ACCOUNT
Put your Writing 4 account in the portfolio, handwritten, about 120 words, with its heading and three paragraphs.
Read it once more before you put it in. Check the six points on the Writing 4 list and correct what you find.

PART 3. THE A2 CHECK: FOUR RESULTS, FOUR LINES
Write these four lines on the back of the card. Do not add them together.
Listening: your score from Practice 6, out of 9.
Reading: your score from the ten comprehension questions, out of 10.
Speaking: your score from Speaking 6, out of 5.
Writing: your score from the Writing 4 checklist, out of 6.
One number for four skills would hide the one that needs your time. Four lines show it.
Under the four lines write one sentence: the skill I will work on first is …

HOW TO CHECK IT YOURSELF
Count three things you can see: four units represented, two recordings present, one handwritten account of about 120 words.
Then play both recordings back and listen for one thing in each: a comparing word after far, much or a lot in Speaking 4, and the five points in Speaking 6.
If somebody is with you, ask them to read the account and tell you what it was about. Doing it alone works too: leave it for a day, then read it as though it were somebody else's.
